text: Will Hicok Low (May 31, 1853 – November 27, 1932) was an American artist, muralist, and writer on art. Born in Albany, New York, he entered the atelier of Jean-Léon Gérôme at the École des Beaux Arts in Paris in 1873 and later joined the classes of Carolus-Duran, remaining with him until 1877. He spent lengthy and painterly periods in Barbizon and Montigny-sur-Loing. Returning to New York, he became a member of the Society of American Artists in 1878 and the National Academy of Design in 1890. His depictions of New England types and illustrations of John Keats brought him recognition. Low created panels and medallions for the Waldorf-Astoria Hotel in New York City, a panel for the Essex County Court House in Newark, New Jersey, and numerous panels for private residences, as well as stained glass windows for various churches, including St. Paul's Methodist Episcopal Church in Newark. He taught at Cooper Union in New York from 1882 to 1885 and at the National Academy of Design from 1889 to 1892. Known as a close friend of R. L. Stevenson, Low published reminiscences titled A Chronicle of Friendships, 1873–1900 (1908). The obverse of the United States silver certificate History Instructing Youth was his design, which was used for the obverse of the bill. The engraving for the obverse of the one-dollar History Instructing Youth note was done by Charles Schlecht. In 1896, he began working for American artist John La Farge, spending two years in New York decorating buildings. After Berthe's death in 1909, he married Mary Fairchild, the former wife of sculptor Frederick William MacMonnies. He painted a series of murals in the New York State Education Department rotunda in Albany, New York, using figures and symbols from Roman and Greek mythology paired with New York buildings and landscapes to chart major milestones in human progress—such as art, science, technology, modernization, liberty, democracy, and quality of life. The earliest panels, including Architecture, Astronomy & Geography, and Medicine & Chemistry, combine theory and practical skills. Another eight panels, such as Theseus, the Pathfinder, feature modern inventions to illustrate human progress by the early 20th century. The final paintings reflect a patriotic theme, with subjects like The Standard, The United States Military Academy, and the Shaft of Union. These murals, originally displayed at the entrances of the State Library Main Reading Room, the Law Library, and the Periodicals Library, complement the Rotunda's architectural nobility and its atmosphere of intellectual enlightenment.
